title: The Start of a Doctor-Pet Relationship
subtitle: A dispatch from The American Telemedicine Association 2026 Nexus Meeting.
body_html:
This is an interview I did just yesterday. I was at the American Telemedicine Annual Meeting in Orlando, and has the pleasure to be speaking about novel regulatory strategies in Software as a Medical Device. I'm on my way to the American Psychiatric Association annual meeting and RAMHT— the sixth version of my live action newsletter event. I met up with somebody who runs fulfillment Pharmacy, and my brain broke a little bit when I learned about the difference between human pharmacy and veterinary pharmacy. It was such a good tidbit that I asked for Cole, the CEO of GOGOMeds to sit down with me for an interview.

Thank you for reading come out and I hope to see you tomorrow night at RAMHT!

The Live-Action Version of this Newsletter, RAMHT 2026 SF, is coming up on May 16th, 2026!

Get Tickets to RAMHT 2026 SF

Owen chat with Cole Maudlin, CEO of GoGoMeds

Owen Muir: Introduce yourself.

Cole Maudlin: I’m the CEO of GoGoMeds.

Owen Muir: What does your company do?

Cole Maudlin: We act as a pharmacy fulfillment partner for any number of services, primarily in the cash-pay healthcare space. For telemedicine companies that want to get into telemedicine, the pharmacy and logistics side is often an afterthought. They pick their go-to-market strategy, figure out what they’re solving in healthcare, and then realize they have to get medication to the patient. We try to get in front of that, because it’s a critical part of the experience.

Owen Muir: Are you a pharmacy?

Cole Maudlin: Effectively, yes. Legally, there is a pharmacy somewhere. We have three: two in Cincinnati, one in Scottsdale, Arizona. They all carry individual pharmacy licenses. We also handle the PIC licenses for each individual state.

Owen Muir: PIC?

Cole Maudlin: Pharmacist in Charge. Each physical pharmacy has to have one. The PIC takes responsibility for anything compliance-related within the four walls of the pharmacy. Some states require that the PIC also be licensed in their state, even if you’re a non-resident pharmacy. A state like Illinois will require that the pharmacist who is the PIC in an Ohio facility also carry an Illinois license.

So we have three physical pharmacies and a significant number of pharmacist licenses. We have tertiary coverage in any state that requires it: a primary PIC, a secondary, and a tertiary. That way we don’t wake up one morning unable to ship medication into a state because a pharmacist is no longer willing or able to be in that role.

Owen Muir: That’s a lot of redundancy.

Cole Maudlin: It is, and you only establish that through experience. You don’t need the second pharmacist until the first one goes out sick. You don’t need the third until the second becomes the primary. Some of that redundancy came from having to shift a PIC from one facility to another, and then realizing the secondary was now at risk.

Owen Muir: There’s so much work to make sure patients get their medications.

Cole Maudlin: There is. From my perspective on the pharmacy side, a lot of people think telemedicine is a more accelerated version of care. It’s actually the opposite. There’s enormous work in systems, compliance, logistics, purchasing, supply chain. Groups that work with us don’t have to manage any of that. I was talking to one of our fulfillment clients, a pretty large company, and I asked if they’d ever open their own pharmacy. They said they didn’t want to be in the business of managing a pharmacy. I said, that’s fair. There are some days I don’t want to be either.

Owen Muir: Every pharmacy board has different requirements?

Cole Maudlin: Yes. North Dakota, for example, still doesn’t allow ED medications to be shipped into the state if the prescription originated through telemedicine.

Owen Muir: Erectile dysfunction medications. You came from a technology background?

Cole Maudlin: I started as CTO of the company. I’m a technologist, not a pharmacist.

Owen Muir: What did you learn from your pharmacist colleagues that surprised you?

Cole Maudlin: One of the things I found really interesting is that people coming from outside the industry, if enabled appropriately, can make meaningful change. When I tried to automate or build software for portions of our pharmacy or fulfillment process and asked why something was done a certain way, the answer was often just, “that’s how it is.” Being able to take a fresh approach to problem-solving in a space where you have no prior experience, only the requirement to build technology for it, was refreshing.

I was also unaware, before this, of all the checks that happen for each individual prescription, and the collaboration required with the prescribing network. There’s almost a collaborative care relationship between the platform, the pharmacy, and the prescriber. It’s a very unique space.

Owen Muir: You also do pharmacy fulfillment for animals. Tell me about that.

Cole Maudlin: There’s a lot of overlap between medications prescribed for humans and for companion animals, primarily dogs and cats. Gabapentin is a peculiar one: a nerve pain medication that is, I think, off-label prescribed for dogs and cats to help manage stress, flights, fireworks, general pet anxiety. And gabapentin is considered a controlled substance in some states but not others. That’s another layer of compliance we manage.

The space is growing. Before Chewy, mail-order veterinary fulfillment was primarily 1-800-PetMeds, a fairly archaic experience. Chewy came in and became the 800-pound gorilla. That forced veterinarians to look at mail-order fulfillment. But what Chewy was doing was bombarding small veterinary offices with phone calls and faxes requesting prescription transfers, which was a loss of revenue for the vet office and also broke the loop of care. The veterinarian loses sight of whether the medication was filled, whether the patient needs a refill, whether it’s time to come back in.

Owen Muir: How did you approach that problem?

Cole Maudlin: Instead of bombarding, we started partnering. We’d go in and talk about an integration, a legal way to move prescriptions from the veterinary office to our pharmacy. Critically, there’s also a revenue-share opportunity for the vet. They can still control a lot of the patient experience. We’ll white-label a website for them. And we provide the data back to the veterinarian: last refill is coming up, last fill date was three months ago, time to get this patient back in front of you.

There’s also no truly adopted e-prescribing clearinghouse in veterinary medicine, nothing like Surescripts. Systems have been built, but veterinary offices haven’t adopted them. Prescription transfers are still heavily phone and fax.

Owen Muir: Tell me about consent. A physician has to see a patient. A veterinarian has to see their patient, which is both the animal and the owner.

Cole Maudlin: In veterinary medicine, a lot of the consent and protections, the equivalent of HIPAA, extend to the owner. The patient-provider relationship on the veterinary side is called the VCPR, Veterinary Client-Patient Relationship. About three years ago, only around 10 states allowed VCPR to be established digitally. Now it’s closer to 40.

Owen Muir: So tele-veterinary medicine exists.

Cole Maudlin: It does. The concept is a bit funny to picture: Spot is on the other side of the camera, and the veterinarian is confirming they’ve evaluated the dog. But it’s legitimate, and there’s legislation around it.

Owen Muir: It’s not unlike pediatrics. You have to see the parent and the child. Assent, consent, and privacy apply to both.

Cole Maudlin: Exactly. And the systems required to facilitate that are remarkably similar. When we built our proprietary platform for human healthcare, we already had the parent-to-child consent relationship. Getting into veterinary meant adding a couple of data fields, mainly weight and species, and having a compliance conversation. We’ve had dogs, cats, birds. I think we’ve even processed a prescription for an ostrich or two.

Owen Muir: What was the biggest surprise in human healthcare when you came in from the outside?

Cole Maudlin: How broken the systems are, and how much common sense can accomplish once you’re inside. Some of the largest direct-to-consumer telemedicine brands probably don’t exist if healthcare isn’t already so dysfunctional, because they’re solving for a broken system, not necessarily for the science or medicine. The pricing is intentionally opaque. PBMs value bottom lines and rebates over patient access. At the end of the day, the consumer and the employer pay for the broken structure. You know it’s a mess from the outside, but until you’re inside trying to fix things with common-sense solutions, you don’t realize how backwards a lot of it is.

Owen Muir: And on the veterinary side?

Cole Maudlin: The pricing, and the overlap in medication. I took my dog in for an antibiotic, and I was smart enough to look at the bottle and think, that looks familiar. I went to our own cash-pay website, looked up the medication, and it was about ten times cheaper than what I’d paid at the vet. I went to one of our PICs and said, are you aware they give this to dogs and cats? She said, oh yes, there’s all kinds of overlap.

Getting into veterinary fulfillment was largely a matter of purchasing the same medications from the same wholesalers we already used and dispensing them to animals. We had to establish a couple of wholesaler accounts for pet-specific medications, but most of it was already there.

Owen Muir: Where can people find GoGoMeds?

Cole Maudlin: GoGoMeds.com.​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​

Thanks for reading, and I hope you enjoy Epcot center in the background.
